content: Wrist fractures, particularly those involving the distal radius, are the most common type of fractures in children. Among these, buckle fractures are the most prevalent and are considered stable fractures, unlike greenstick or other displaced fractures, which are typically less stable. There is significant variability in clinical practice regarding the management of these fractures, including the degree of immobilization required for buckle fractures and the use of surgical interventions for severely displaced fractures. The objective of this review was to evaluate the benefits and harms of various interventions for treating distal radius fractures in children, including skeletally immature adolescents. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-RCTs that compared different treatment approaches. The outcomes assessed included physical function, treatment failure, adverse events, recovery time, wrist pain, and satisfaction of both the child and their parents. A total of 30 studies were included, involving 2930 children, with most studies recruiting more male participants and reporting mean ages between 8 and 10 years. The studies addressed different types of fractures, including buckle fractures, minimally displaced fractures, and displaced fractures requiring closed reduction. All studies were at high risk of bias, primarily due to the lack of blinding. The review identified 14 treatment comparisons, with five key comparisons summarized below: 1. Removable splint versus below-elbow cast for buckle fractures: Six studies involving 695 children were included. One study reported similar physical function scores at four weeks, with low-quality evidence. Device changes or reapplications were required in 13 children across four studies, with very low-quality evidence. No refractures were reported at six months in one study. Pain levels during treatment were similar between groups, but the evidence was of very low quality. Data on recovery time, minor complications, and satisfaction were either absent, insufficient, or contradictory. Two studies suggested lower healthcare costs for removable splints. 2. Soft or elasticated bandage versus below-elbow cast for buckle or similar fractures: Four studies involving 273 children were included. One study reported that more children in the bandage group had no or limited disability at four weeks, but the evidence was of very low quality. Device changes or extended immobilization for delayed union occurred in eight children across three studies, with very low-quality evidence. No serious adverse events were reported at four weeks in two studies. Evidence on recovery time, wrist pain, minor complications, and satisfaction was either absent, insufficient, or contradictory. More participants in the bandage group found their treatment convenient. 3. Removal of casts at home by parents versus at the hospital fracture clinic by clinicians: Two studies involving 404 children, mostly with buckle fractures, were included. One study reported full restoration of physical function at four weeks, with low-quality evidence. Five treatment changes were reported across two studies, with very low-quality evidence. No serious adverse effects were reported at six months in one study. Recovery time and minor complications were not reported. Pain levels at four weeks were similar between groups, with low-quality evidence. One study found greater parental satisfaction in the home group, with low-quality evidence. A UK study reported lower healthcare costs for home removal. 4. Below-elbow versus above-elbow casts for displaced or unstable both-bone fractures: Four studies involving 399 children were included. Short-term physical function data were unavailable, but very low-quality evidence suggested less dependency with below-elbow casts. One study reported minimal differences in functional scores for minimally displaced fractures. Treatment failure data were unavailable, but nine of 11 remanipulations occurred in the above-elbow group, with very low-quality evidence. No refractures or compartment syndrome were reported at six months. Recovery time and minor complications were not reported. One study found less pain at one week with below-elbow casts, with low-quality evidence. Treatment with above-elbow casts was three times more expensive in one study conducted in Nepal. 5. Surgical fixation with percutaneous wiring and cast immobilization versus cast immobilization alone after closed reduction of displaced fractures: Five studies involving 323 children were included. Short-term functional outcome data were unavailable. One study reported similar functional scores at six months, with low-quality evidence. Fewer treatment failures and serious adverse events were reported after surgery, with very low-quality evidence. Recovery time, wrist pain, and satisfaction were not reported. One study found lower referral rates for physiotherapy for stiffness after surgery, with very low-quality evidence. A study in the USA reported similar treatment costs between the two groups. The authors concluded that the quality of evidence from RCTs on interventions for treating wrist fractures in children is generally low or very low. However, there is reassuring evidence that correctly diagnosed buckle fractures, regardless of treatment, result in a full return to previous function without serious adverse events, including refractures. These findings support the trend away from cast immobilization for buckle fractures. High-quality evidence is needed to address key uncertainties in treatment, and ongoing multicenter trials, such as the FORCE trial, are expected to provide further insights.
